belfast.intro: Belfast's oldest tree is an oak, and nobody has settled which oak it is. The Belvoir Oak, in a forest park in the south, is called the oldest living oak in Ireland by the department that manages the ground, though two veterans stand near the Motte. The Botanic Gardens hold a 400-year-old Australian grass tree under glass, a hornbeam that may date from the gardens' founding in 1828 and a plane crusted with burrs. A short walk away, a young plane said to descend from Hippocrates' tree on Kos won Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2017.
belfast.meta_description: Belfast's old trees: an oak called the oldest in Ireland, a 400-year-old grass tree under glass, and a plane said to descend from Hippocrates' tree.
belfast.question_meta: Belfast's oldest tree is the Belvoir Oak, put at 400 to 600 years. Which of two veteran oaks near the Motte carries the name is still unsettled.
belfast.question_answer: The oldest tree in Belfast is the Belvoir Oak in Belvoir Park Forest, in the south of the city. DAERA, the government department that manages the forest, calls it the oldest living oak in Ireland at 500 to 600 years old; a senior ranger who assessed it in 2016 said more than 400 and that its condition makes an exact age impossible, so the honest band is 400 to 600. It stands near the Motte, roughly a 15 minute walk from Galwally halt, and the pin here marks the forest rather than the trunk.
belfast.question_context:
There is an unresolved question sitting under that answer, and it is worth knowing before the walk. Robert Welch photographed a great oak in Belvoir Park Forest more than a century ago, already well over 300 years old and known locally as Granddad. Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees project states plainly that Granddad may not be the same specimen as the tree now promoted as the Belvoir Oak, which means two distinct veterans may stand near the Motte, one of them seriously declined and the other healthier and better publicised. Nobody has settled it in public, and a reader who walks that ground can probably settle it faster than we can.

One rival for the title is not an oak and not a tree. The Australian grass tree inside the Palm House at the Botanic Gardens is put at over 400 years, which overlaps the oak's range, and it is a monocot rather than a tree in the usual sense. The gardens' hornbeam may date from their founding in 1828, but that is the gardens' belief rather than a record. On the numbers as they stand the oak takes it, on a range that runs from 400 years to 600.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Belfast?
faq.a: The Belvoir Oak in Belvoir Park Forest. DAERA calls it the oldest living oak in Ireland at 500 to 600 years; a 2016 ranger assessment says more than 400 and that the tree's condition makes an exact figure impossible. The honest band is 400 to 600.

faq.q: Are Belfast's old trees free to visit?
faq.a: All of them are free. Belvoir Park Forest is open around the clock, and the Botanic Gardens and the Palm House cost nothing to enter. Friar's Bush Graveyard is free too, though it is kept locked and you book a slot with Belfast City Council first. The Hippocrates plane stands in Belfast City Hospital grounds, where we have not confirmed open access to the lawn.

faq.q: Is there really a tree from Hippocrates in Belfast?
faq.a: By the hospital's tradition, yes. In the late 1960s a Greek kidney doctor at Belfast City Hospital, Dimitrios Oreopoulos, had seeds of the Plane Tree of Kos planted, and the survivor behind Erskine House was voted Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2017. Its descent from the Kos tree has never been tested.

faq.q: How do you get into Friar's Bush Graveyard?
faq.a: By arranging it first. Belfast City Council manages the site and admits visitors on a booked slot, by telephone on 028 9027 0296 or by email; Cairde na Cille and the Friends of Friar's Bush Graveyard also run guided tours. Turning up unannounced gets you a look at the wall.

faq.q: Is the grass tree in the Palm House really a tree?
faq.a: No. Xanthorrhoea preissii is an Australian monocot in the asphodel family, no closer to an oak than a lily is. It grows a dark trunk of packed old leaf bases, it is the oldest living thing in the Botanic Gardens, and it is worth the detour precisely because it is odd.

florence-court.intro: Florence Court, a National Trust estate in Fermanagh, holds the tree every Irish yew in the world is said to descend from. It is not a tall column but a low, scraggy survivor beside a stream in a glade, cut back for two centuries of cuttings. A farmer found it as a wild seedling on the slopes of Cuilcagh before 1767, perhaps as early as 1740, and gave it to his landlord. That makes it at least about 250 years old.
florence-court.meta_description: The Florence Court Yew, Fermanagh: the scraggy tree every Irish yew is said to descend from, at least 250 years old. National Trust, paid entry.
florence-court.question_meta: Florence Court's remarkable tree is the original Irish yew, said to be the parent of every Irish yew, at least about 250 years old.
florence-court.question_answer: Florence Court's notable tree is the Florence Court Yew, the original Irish yew, said to be the parent of every Irish yew growing anywhere. It stands beside a small stream in a glade on the National Trust's Florence Court estate, south-west of Enniskillen.
florence-court.question_context: The tree began wild. A farmer, George Willis, found two upright yew seedlings on the slopes of Cuilcagh, at a rock called Carraig-na-madadh, the Rock of the Dog, and gave one to his landlord, Lord Mountflorence, later Earl of Enniskillen. Only this one survives. The date is disputed. Sources give 1740, 1760, 1764, 1767 and 1780, and the Fermanagh botanists put the collecting before 1767, which makes the planted tree at least about 250 years old. The Irish yews in churchyards everywhere are said to be cuttings of this one. It shows the cost. The botanists who know it say it survives rather than thrives, scraggy and lichen-covered, long shaded by ash and sycamore. Clearing and pruning in 1980 helped, and it was reported stable in 2010, the last dated condition report we could read. Florence Court is a National Trust property with paid entry for non-members, and Storm Eowyn damaged the Trust's estates here in January 2025.

faq.q: Where is the original Irish yew?
faq.a: At Florence Court in County Fermanagh, about 12 km south-west of Enniskillen, beside a small stream in a glade on the National Trust estate.

faq.q: How old is the Florence Court Yew?
faq.a: At least about 250 years. It was collected as a wild seedling before 1767, perhaps as early as 1740; sources disagree on the year.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see the Florence Court Yew?
faq.a: Yes, unless you are a National Trust member. Florence Court charges non-members for entry; check the current price and hours on the National Trust site before travelling.

faq.q: Why does the Florence Court Yew look so small?
faq.a: It has been cut for cuttings for two centuries and was long shaded by taller trees. The botanists who know it say it survives rather than thrives.

crom.intro: Crom is a National Trust estate on Upper Lough Erne in Fermanagh, and its famous trees are two old yews at the ruins of a castle built in 1611 and burnt in the 1760s. They are said to have marked the entrance to the old castle garden. Lord Erne is said to put them at 800 years, other guesses run from 400 to 1,000, and nobody has settled it. The larger measured 474 cm round in 2000.
crom.meta_description: The Crom Yews, Fermanagh: two old yews at the ruins of a 1611 castle, ages claimed from 400 to 1,000 years. National Trust estate, paid entry.
crom.question_meta: Crom's remarkable trees are two old yews at the ruins of Old Crom Castle, with ages claimed from 400 to 1,000 years and none proven.
crom.question_answer: Crom's notable trees are the Crom Yews, a pair of old yews at the ruins of Old Crom Castle on the National Trust's Crom Estate, near Newtownbutler in County Fermanagh. Their age is disputed and has never been measured.
crom.question_context: The old castle at Crom was built in 1611, during the Plantation of Ulster, and burnt in the early 1760s. The two yews beside its ruins are said to have marked the entrance to its garden, which is long gone. How old they are is the open question. Lord Erne is said to claim 800 years. A National Trust trail guide, by a summary we could not read in full, gives anything from 400 to 1,000, and the Trust admits the debate has run for years. We leave the age open. The earliest written mention we found is J.C. Loudon's, in 1837. The measurements come from the Tree Register of Ireland's record of 2000. The larger yew 474 cm round at 10 cm above the ground and 10.8 metres tall, the smaller 430 cm round and 14 metres tall. Photographs show branches that have rooted where they touch the ground. We found no measurement since. The estate was given to the National Trust by the 6th Earl of Erne in 1987. Some trees here are so old that access to them is restricted, so expect to look from the path.

faq.q: How old are the Crom Yews?
faq.a: Nobody knows. Lord Erne is said to claim 800 years and other estimates run from 400 to 1,000. None of them is a measured age.

faq.q: Can you get close to the Crom Yews?
faq.a: Some of Crom's oldest trees have restricted access, so plan to view them from the path at the Old Crom Castle ruins.

faq.q: Is Crom free to visit?
faq.a: National Trust members get in free; non-members pay. Opening hours differ between listings, and Storm Eowyn changed some routes in 2025, so check the National Trust page first.

faq.q: How do you get to Crom?
faq.a: Realistically by car. Crom is about 5 km from Newtownbutler and roughly 25 km south-east of Enniskillen, with no useful public transport.

dark-hedges.intro: The Dark Hedges is an avenue of beeches over the Bregagh Road near Armoy, in County Antrim, planted by the Stuart family around 1775 along the drive to Gracehill House. Game of Thrones made it famous as the King's Road. Storms have felled beeches almost every year since 2016, and the road has been closed to traffic since 2017, so you walk it. The trees stand on private land either side of the public road.
dark-hedges.meta_description: The Dark Hedges, County Antrim: beeches planted around 1775, thinned by storms since 2016. Free to walk; the road is closed to traffic since 2017.
dark-hedges.question_meta: The Dark Hedges is an avenue of beeches planted around 1775 near Armoy, closed to traffic since 2017 and thinned by storms since 2016.
dark-hedges.question_answer: The Dark Hedges is an avenue of beech trees arching over the Bregagh Road near Armoy in County Antrim, planted around 1775 along the drive to Gracehill House. It is free to walk, closed to traffic since 2017, and the trees stand on private land beside the road.
dark-hedges.question_context: The Stuart family planted about 150 beeches along the entrance road to Gracehill House around 1775, and over two and a half centuries the crowns grew together into a tunnel. After Game of Thrones filmed it as the King's Road, visitor numbers rose sharply. The storms came at the same time. Gertrude took two in 2016, Doris one in 2017, Hector one in 2018, an unnamed gale one in 2019, Arwen two in 2021, Isha three in 2024 and Eowyn two in January 2025, and others have been felled for safety. How many remain is not settled. A 2023 survey reported 86 and a more recent tally says around 75. The trees have had a preservation order since 2004 and a preservation trust since 2009. On 30 October 2017 the stretch between Ballinlea Road and Ballykenver Road was closed to all but emergency and farm vehicles, after the 2016 losses and the weight of traffic. The road is public; the land the beeches stand on is not. Look from the road and stay out of the fields. Walkers are sometimes kept out too, while tree work goes on.

faq.q: Can you drive through the Dark Hedges?
faq.a: No. Bregagh Road between Ballinlea Road and Ballykenver Road has been closed to traffic since 30 October 2017, except for emergency and farm vehicles. Park at the Ballinlea Road end and walk.

faq.q: How many trees are left at the Dark Hedges?
faq.a: Fewer every few years. About 150 were planted around 1775; a 2023 survey counted 86 and a later tally says around 75. Storms have taken beeches almost every year since 2016.

faq.q: Is the Dark Hedges free?
faq.a: Yes. It is a public road. The beeches stand on private land beside it, so look from the road and do not go into the fields.

faq.q: How old are the Dark Hedges?
faq.a: About 250 years. The avenue was planted around 1775 by the Stuart family along the drive to Gracehill House.

faq.q: Can you get to the Dark Hedges by bus?
faq.a: Not easily. It is about 3 km from Armoy and 15 km from Ballymoney, and rural Translink services are infrequent. Most visitors come by car or on a coach tour.

rostrevor.intro: Rostrevor is a village on Carlingford Lough in County Down, and Kilbroney Park above it holds Old Homer, a holm oak that grows at roughly 45 degrees. It won Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2016 with more than half the vote and came sixth in Europe the next year. In 2020 the council took close to two tons off its crown to stop it falling. The park is free and open all year.
rostrevor.meta_description: Old Homer, Kilbroney Park, Rostrevor: a leaning holm oak about 200 years old, Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year 2016. Free, open all year.
rostrevor.question_meta: Rostrevor's remarkable tree is Old Homer, a holm oak leaning at about 45 degrees in Kilbroney Park, Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year 2016.
rostrevor.question_answer: Rostrevor's notable tree is Old Homer, a holm oak that leans at roughly 45 degrees just inside the Fairy Glen entrance to Kilbroney Park. It is about 200 years old and was voted Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2016.
rostrevor.question_context: Old Homer took more than half the public vote in the Woodland Trust's Northern Ireland contest in 2016, and in 2017 it came sixth of sixteen in the European Tree of the Year with 7,101 votes. It was planted about 200 years ago, the Irish News reports, by the Ross family, when Kilbroney was their private estate rather than a council park. The trunk is a little under four metres round, with bark like snakeskin. The lean that makes it famous nearly ended it. In July 2020 a councillor warned that splits and cracks at the base meant it might not survive the next snowfall, and weeks later the council had the crown reduced by close to two tons and declared it saved, with a support underneath planned. One bough has since been propped. The last report on the tree itself that we found is from 2020 and early 2021, so a recent sighting is welcome. Kilbroney Park is council land, free and open every day from 9 am, and the Fairy Glen entrance is about ten minutes on foot from the village.

faq.q: Where is Old Homer?
faq.a: Just inside the Fairy Glen pedestrian entrance to Kilbroney Park, Rostrevor, County Down, about ten minutes' walk from the village.

faq.q: Why does Old Homer lean?
faq.a: Nobody has published why. It grows at roughly 45 degrees, and in 2020 the lean and cracks at its base led the council to remove close to two tons from the crown.

faq.q: Is Kilbroney Park free?
faq.a: Yes. It is a council park, open year round from 9 am.

faq.q: How old is Old Homer?
faq.a: About 200 years. The Irish News reports it was planted by the Ross family when the park was their private estate.

castlewellan.intro: Castlewellan Forest Park, in County Down, keeps its oldest conifers in the walled Annesley Garden and arboretum. A giant sequoia planted as a sapling in 1856 has grown nineteen trunks and was Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2018. Near the entrance path a pair of redwoods faces each other, one of them named the most gigantic in Ulster. The garden also bred the golden Leyland cypress sold as Castlewellan Gold. Entry is free on foot.
castlewellan.meta_description: Castlewellan Forest Park, County Down: a 19-trunk sequoia from 1856, Ulster's biggest redwood and the first Castlewellan Gold. Free on foot.
castlewellan.question_meta: Castlewellan's remarkable trees are 19th-century giant sequoias in the Annesley Garden, one with 19 trunks, Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year 2018.
castlewellan.question_answer: Castlewellan's best-known tree is the multi-stemmed giant sequoia in the walled Annesley Garden, planted as a sapling in 1856 and grown into nineteen trunks. Northern Ireland voted it Tree of the Year in 2018. The oldest documented trees in the park are its sequoias, more than 160 years old.
castlewellan.question_context: The park's giant sequoias grew from seed William Lobb brought from California in 1853 for the Veitch nurseries, planted out as saplings in 1856. The multi-stemmed tree is the best recorded of them. The 5th Earl Annesley photographed it in 1871 at fifteen years old, and its lower branches have since layered and rooted until it stands on nineteen trunks. Near the arboretum's entrance path, beside formal steps, two more redwoods face each other across the path. Northern Ireland's Forest Service book calls one of them the most gigantic of Ulster's redwoods, and gives one of the pair a girth of 22 feet 2 inches without making clear which. Their own planting date is not recorded. The garden is also where the park's director, John Keown, spotted the golden seedling that became the hedge plant Castlewellan Gold, named in 1963; whether the original still stands has not been confirmed recently. A California nutmeg here is called the tallest of its kind in Britain and Ireland, on measurements from 1982, and nobody has published where it stands. Recent sightings of any of them are welcome.

faq.q: Is Castlewellan Forest Park free?
faq.a: Free on foot. Cars pay a charge at the park; the amount is on the nidirect page for Castlewellan Forest Park.

faq.q: When is the Annesley Garden open?
faq.a: Daily from 10 am until sunset. The walled garden is reached through the forest park.

faq.q: How old are the sequoias at Castlewellan?
faq.a: More than 160 years. They grew from seed brought from California in 1853 and were planted out as saplings in 1856.

faq.q: Is the original Castlewellan Gold still there?
faq.a: Probably, but we have no recent dated sighting. It is said to stand in the ornamental gardens near the Heron Fountain; if you see it, tell us.

faq.q: How do you get to Castlewellan Forest Park by bus?
faq.a: Ulsterbus services between Newcastle and Newry stop in Castlewellan village, about 1.5 km from the park entrance.

armagh.intro: Armagh's Mall is an oval public park laid out in the late 18th century and still lined with protected trees and Georgian buildings. One of its horse chestnuts, a veteran known to a neighbour since childhood as the King Tree, was shortlisted for Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2019. Nobody has published which trunk it is, or its age, so the walk ends in a question for anyone local.
armagh.meta_description: The King Tree, Armagh: a veteran horse chestnut on the Georgian Mall, shortlisted for NI Tree of the Year 2019. Free, in the city centre.
armagh.question_meta: Armagh's remarkable tree is the King Tree, a veteran horse chestnut on the Mall, shortlisted for Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2019.
armagh.question_answer: Armagh's notable tree is the King Tree, a veteran horse chestnut on the Mall in the city centre, shortlisted for Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year in 2019. Its age has never been published, and no source says exactly which trunk on the Mall it is.
armagh.question_context: The Mall is the long oval park at the heart of Armagh, laid out for the public in the late 18th century and framed by Georgian buildings. Its trees are protected; in 2020 the council scheduled works on 21 of them and removed a hollow lime at the Gaol end. The King Tree got its name from someone who grew up in a Georgian house across the road and has called it that since childhood. In 2019 it was nominated for the Woodland Trust's Northern Ireland Tree of the Year and made the shortlist, described as a primary veteran horse chestnut. That shortlist is the only source we have. It gives no age, girth or planting date, and it does not place the tree among its neighbours, so our pin sits in the middle of the Mall rather than on the trunk. The last confirmation that the tree stands is also from 2019. That is a gap a local can close in five minutes. If you know which chestnut it is, a photograph and a word would put the pin in the right place. The Mall is free and a few minutes from the bus station.

faq.q: Where is the King Tree in Armagh?
faq.a: On the Mall in the centre of Armagh. No source says which of the Mall's horse chestnuts it is, so our pin marks the park, not the trunk.

faq.q: How old is the King Tree?
faq.a: Nobody has published an age. It was described as a primary veteran horse chestnut when it was shortlisted in 2019.

faq.q: Is the Mall in Armagh free?
faq.a: Yes. It is open public ground in the city centre, a few minutes' walk from the bus station on Dobbin Street.

gosford.intro: Gosford Forest Park, outside Markethill in County Armagh, has a quiet grassy arboretum, and its champion is a Himalayan fir that Northern Ireland's Forest Service book says holds the record for the greatest girth of its species, 13 feet 10 inches round. The measurement is undated and the book is the only source, so a recent sighting is welcome. It keeps company with veteran Douglas firs with craggy bark.
gosford.meta_description: The Gosford Champion Fir, County Armagh: a Himalayan fir listed with the greatest girth of its species, 4.2 metres round. Forest park, car charge.
gosford.question_meta: Gosford's remarkable tree is a Himalayan fir in the forest park arboretum, listed in the record books for the greatest girth of its species.
gosford.question_answer: Gosford Forest Park's notable tree is the champion Himalayan fir, Abies spectabilis, in the arboretum near Markethill, County Armagh. Northern Ireland's Forest Service book says it is in the record books for the greatest girth of its species, 13 feet 10 inches, about 4.2 metres.
gosford.question_context: Almost everything known about this tree comes from one source, Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees, a Forest Service book published some time between about 2005 and 2015. It names the Himalayan fir as the arboretum's champion, gives its girth as 13 feet 10 inches, calls it extremely tall and says it was in excellent health when the book was written. It does not date the measurement and gives no height. Nobody has dated the tree. We found no report of it falling, and none confirming it stands today, which is why the entry carries a flag. The setting is described in more detail than the tree. It is a quiet, grassy arboretum with the trees well spaced, and a group of veteran Douglas firs whose bark has gone craggy and carbuncled. Our pin marks the middle of the forest park rather than the fir, so allow time to look. If you find it, a photograph and a position would help the next visitor more than anything we could add. The park is run by the Forest Service and open to the public, with a charge for cars.

faq.q: Is Gosford Forest Park free?
faq.a: It is open to the public on foot, and cars pay a charge. Check the nidirect page for Gosford Forest Park before travelling.

faq.q: Where in Gosford is the champion fir?
faq.a: In the arboretum. No source gives its exact position, so our pin marks the forest park, not the tree.

faq.q: How do you get to Gosford Forest Park by bus?
faq.a: Ulsterbus services between Armagh and Newry call at Markethill, about 2 km from the park entrance.

reelig-glen.intro: Reelig Glen, a wooded glen about seven miles west of Inverness, holds two of the tallest trees in Britain. Dughall Mor, a Douglas fir measured at 62 metres in 2000, was once the tallest known. A neighbour about 55 yards away was measured at 66.4 metres in 2014 and reported as the UK's tallest tree. Every tree in the stand is over a century old, and the waymarked Tall Trees Walk is free.
reelig-glen.meta_description: Reelig Glen, near Inverness: Douglas firs including one measured at 66.4 metres in 2014, reported as the UK's tallest tree. Free woodland walk.
reelig-glen.question_meta: Reelig Glen's remarkable trees are giant Douglas firs, one measured at 66.4 m in 2014 and reported as the UK's tallest, beside the former champion.
reelig-glen.question_answer: Reelig Glen's notable trees are its giant Douglas firs, above all the Reelig Glen Fir, measured at 66.4 metres in 2014 and reported as the tallest tree in the UK, and Dughall Mor, about 55 yards away, which held the title before it. Wikipedia's list of superlative trees gives them 66.3 and 63.8 metres.
reelig-glen.question_context: Dughall Mor, Gaelic for Big Douglas, took its name from a local competition and was measured at 62 metres in 2000 and reported at 64 in 2005, when no taller tree was known in Britain. In 2014 its neighbour was measured by laser and by climbing at 66.4 metres, and the newspapers moved the title down the path. Heights this great shift with the method and the year, so read the two as a close race rather than a fixed order. The glen itself was planted from the 1800s by the Fraser family, much of it credited to James Baillie Fraser, a traveller in the Himalaya, and the Forestry Commission bought it in 1949. Every tree in the stand is over a century old, and many are around 50 metres. One list dates Dughall Mor to 1882, which we could not confirm. The catch is telling the two apart. A bark label on Dughall Mor was reported missing in 2022, and a walker that year could not be sure which trunk was which. The waymarked Tall Trees Walk is about a mile, free, from the Reelig Glen car park off the A862.

faq.q: What is the tallest tree in Reelig Glen?
faq.a: The Reelig Glen Fir, a Douglas fir measured at 66.4 metres in 2014 and reported then as the tallest tree in the UK. Wikipedia's list now gives 66.3 metres.

faq.q: Is Reelig Glen free?
faq.a: Yes, it is a Forestry and Land Scotland woodland and free to walk. Parking charges apply at some of their sites, so check before going.

faq.q: How long is the walk at Reelig Glen?
faq.a: The waymarked Tall Trees Walk is about a mile from the car park, along the Moniack Burn.

faq.q: Can you get to Reelig Glen by bus?
faq.a: Not usefully. It is about seven miles west of Inverness and most visitors drive to the car park.

inverness.intro: Our tree near Inverness is the Lord President's Oak in Culloden Wood, about five miles east of the city. It is said to have been planted around 1855, when a stone seat used by Duncan Forbes, Lord President of the Court of Session, had to be moved for the Highland railway. Forestry and Land Scotland nominated it for Scotland's Tree of the Year in 2020. The woodland trail is free.
inverness.meta_description: The Lord President's Oak, Culloden Wood near Inverness: planted around 1855 beside a moved stone seat. Nominated for Tree of the Year 2020. Free.
inverness.question_meta: Near Inverness, the Lord President's Oak in Culloden Wood is a 19th-century oak beside a stone seat moved for the Highland railway in 1855.
inverness.question_answer: Our tree near Inverness is the Lord President's Oak in Culloden Wood, about five miles east of the city, on the trail to St Mary's Well. It was planted around 1855, by the wood's own account, and Forestry and Land Scotland nominated it for Scotland's Tree of the Year in 2020.
inverness.question_context: The oak takes its name from the boulder beneath it, the Lord President's Seat. Duncan Forbes of Culloden, Lord President of the Court of Session, who died in 1747, is said to have sat on it with his wife. In 1855 the stone had to be moved for the Highland railway, and the oak was planted beside it around the same time, which puts the tree at roughly 170 years. That planting story comes from a single nomination, so read it as the wood's tradition. In 2020 Forestry and Land Scotland put the tree forward for Scotland's Tree of the Year and called it one of the most impressive in the country. It is not a veteran, and nobody has published which oak it is, sessile or pedunculate, or its girth, so a reader with a tape measure can add more than we can. A walker in 2024 described the boulder below an old tree, which is our most recent sighting. The trail also passes the Prisoners' Stone and St Mary's clootie well, and starts from the Culloden Wood car park. It is free.

faq.q: Where is the Lord President's Oak?
faq.a: In Culloden Wood, about five miles east of Inverness, at the Lord President's Seat, a boulder just south of the railway bridge on the trail to St Mary's Well.

faq.q: How old is the Lord President's Oak?
faq.a: Roughly 170 years, if the story that it was planted around 1855 holds. That date comes from a single nomination, not a planting record.

faq.q: Is Culloden Wood free?
faq.a: Yes. It is a Forestry and Land Scotland woodland, walked on foot from the Culloden Wood car park.

faq.q: Can you get to Culloden Wood by bus from Inverness?
faq.a: Buses run from Inverness to Culloden village, from where you walk into the wood; check the current timetable.

ardkinglas.intro: Ardkinglas, at Cairndow on the head of Loch Fyne, has a woodland garden with two record conifers. A grand fir planted around 1875 was Britain's tallest tree for a number of years, the estate says, and stood at 64.8 metres in 2025. A silver fir nearly ten metres round is called by the estate the mightiest conifer in Europe. The garden is open in daylight all year; check the admission price with the estate.
ardkinglas.meta_description: Ardkinglas Woodland Garden, Loch Fyne: a grand fir 64.8 m tall and a silver fir nearly 10 m round, called Europe's mightiest conifer.
ardkinglas.question_meta: Ardkinglas's remarkable trees are a grand fir once Britain's tallest, 64.8 m in 2025, and a silver fir nearly 10 m round.
ardkinglas.question_answer: Ardkinglas Woodland Garden, at Cairndow on Loch Fyne, has two notable trees, a grand fir planted around 1875 and measured by the estate at 64.8 metres in July 2025, once Britain's tallest tree, and a silver fir nearly ten metres round that the estate calls the mightiest conifer in Europe.
ardkinglas.question_context: The grand fir went into the lower woodland garden, the Pinetum, as a sapling around 1875. It was recorded at 203 feet in 2002, 64.28 metres when climbed in 2010 and 64.8 metres by the estate in 2025. For years it was Britain's tallest tree, the estate says, until a Douglas fir at Reelig Glen near Inverness was measured at 66.4 metres. The silver fir is the older and wider of the two. The estate puts it at about 250 years, a figure only the owner gives, with a trunk nearly ten metres round; Wikipedia says over 31 feet. Accounts describe the trunk dividing into several great stems, and the name, the mightiest conifer, was given by the 10th Duke of Argyll more than a hundred years ago. No height is published for it, and neither tree's exact spot is mapped, so our pins mark the garden. The grand fir is reached along the Window Walk, high above the water, a few minutes from the lochan and the weir bridge. Paths are hilly, with steep steps and roots. We could not find the admission price, so ring the estate office on 01499 600261 first.

faq.q: What is the tallest tree at Ardkinglas?
faq.a: The grand fir in the Pinetum, measured by the estate at 64.8 metres in July 2025. It was Britain's tallest tree for a number of years, until a Douglas fir at Reelig Glen was measured at 66.4 metres.

faq.q: Is Ardkinglas Woodland Garden open all year?
faq.a: It has been open all year in daylight hours. Admission prices are not published where we could read them; check ardkinglas.com or the estate office before you go.

faq.q: How big is the Ardkinglas silver fir?
faq.a: Nearly ten metres round by the estate's measure, over 31 feet by Wikipedia's. The estate calls it the mightiest conifer in Europe and puts it at about 250 years.

faq.q: How do you get to Ardkinglas?
faq.a: It is at Cairndow on the A83, with a car park at the woodland garden. The Citylink coach from Glasgow to Campbeltown stops at Cairndow; check the timetable.

glen-affric.intro: Glen Affric's tree is the Last Ent of Affric, a lone wych elm growing out of a mountain stream in Gleann nan Cichean, a side glen far beyond the end of the road. It is hundreds of years old, 3.8 metres round, and may be the last survivor of an ancient forest. It was Scotland's Tree of the Year in 2019. Reaching it is a long hill walk or bike ride with no waymarked path.
glen-affric.meta_description: The Last Ent of Affric, Glen Affric: a lone wych elm hundreds of years old, Scotland's Tree of the Year 2019. Free, about 11 km beyond the road end.
glen-affric.question_meta: Glen Affric's remarkable tree is the Last Ent of Affric, a lone wych elm hundreds of years old, about 11 km beyond the end of the road.
glen-affric.question_answer: Glen Affric's notable tree is the Last Ent of Affric, a lone wych elm in Gleann nan Cichean, a side glen of Glen Affric near Cannich. Forestry and Land Scotland calls it hundreds of years old, and it was Scotland's Tree of the Year in 2019.
glen-affric.question_context: The elm grows on the rocky outflow of a mountain stream, with almost no soil under the moss, and it may be the last survivor of an ancient forest. Its isolation, many miles from the next elm, is credited by Wikipedia with keeping it free of Dutch elm disease. Nobody has dated it more closely than hundreds of years. The trunk is 3.8 metres round at chest height. The name comes from Tolkien's Ents, and in 2019 Forestry and Land Scotland nominated it for Scotland's Tree of the Year, which it won in a public vote. In April 2024 the forestry body planted 35 young wych elms from the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh beside it, inside a deer fence, the first of about 200 planned over two years. Getting there is a commitment. Forestry and Land Scotland puts it about 11 kilometres beyond the end of the road, with no waymarked path, and the road end is itself 13 kilometres of single-track from Cannich. Plan it as a long hill walk or bike ride, and turn back after storms if the way looks unsafe.

faq.q: Where is the Last Ent of Affric?
faq.a: In Gleann nan Cichean, a side glen of Glen Affric, about 11 km beyond the end of the road, according to Forestry and Land Scotland. The pin marks the tree.

faq.q: Is there a path to the Last Ent of Affric?
faq.a: No waymarked path that we found. It is a long hill walk or bike ride from the Glen Affric road end; go prepared.

faq.q: How old is the Last Ent of Affric?
faq.a: Hundreds of years, Forestry and Land Scotland says. Nobody has dated it more precisely.

faq.q: Can you get to Glen Affric by public transport?
faq.a: Buses from Inverness reach Cannich, but we found none to the road end, 13 km further by single-track road.

benmore.intro: Benmore Botanic Garden, north of Dunoon in Argyll, opens with an avenue of giant sequoias planted in 1863 by James Piers Patrick, an American who had bought the estate the year before. The trees now stand about 50 metres tall, but the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh says their crowns are thinning and has been treating the soil since 2021. Entry is paid, and the garden opens from March to October.
benmore.meta_description: Benmore Redwood Avenue, Argyll: giant sequoias planted in 1863, now about 50 metres tall. Paid entry, open March to October.
benmore.question_meta: Benmore's remarkable trees are its avenue of giant sequoias, planted in 1863 and about 50 m tall, just inside the botanic garden's entrance.
benmore.question_answer: Benmore's notable trees are the giant sequoias of the Redwood Avenue, lining the original drive to Benmore House just inside the entrance of Benmore Botanic Garden, near Dunoon. They were planted in 1863 and are about 50 metres tall.
benmore.question_context: James Piers Patrick, an American, bought the Benmore estate in 1862 and planted the avenue the following year, from seed William Lobb had brought to Britain. More than 160 years later the trees line the first stretch of any visit. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, which runs Benmore, puts them at about 50 metres; other sources say over 40 or over 45. They are struggling. The garden says the crowns are thinning, the lower branches have lost their needles and the soil is compacted, and that the trees are merely existing rather than growing. Since February 2021 it has treated the ground with geo-injection and air-lancing, and it plans a drainage raft under the grassed length of the avenue, with a public appeal for the work. The number of trees in the avenue is not settled. Figures from 49 to over 150 circulate and the garden gives none. Entry is paid, children 15 and under go free, and the garden opens daily from 1 March to 31 October. Buses run from Dunoon, about twenty minutes by ferry from Gourock.

faq.q: How much does Benmore Botanic Garden cost?
faq.a: When we checked in November 2026, adults paid 12 pounds with Gift Aid and concessions 10; children 15 and under and RBGE members go free.

faq.q: When is Benmore Botanic Garden open?
faq.a: Daily from 10 am to 5 pm between 1 March and 31 October. It is closed in winter and reopens on 1 March 2027.

faq.q: How old are the Benmore redwoods?
faq.a: They were planted in 1863, so a little over 160 years.

faq.q: How do you get to Benmore without a car?
faq.a: Take the CalMac or Western Ferries crossing from Gourock to Dunoon, about 20 minutes, then the West Coast Motors bus seven miles north on the A815.
